explain.say: Here are smart promise steps: think first, can I really do this? Promise clearly, write it down, do it, and if you cannot, tell them early. Great listening! Fun fact: in Japan a pinky promise is called yubikiri.

steps.ask: When should I not make a promise?

steps.label: Promise clearly
steps.note: Say exactly what you will do.

steps.label: Cannot? Say so
steps.note: Tell them early and say sorry.
steps.ask: What if I really cannot keep a promise?

faq.q: How does it feel when someone breaks a promise?
faq.a: It can feel sad, disappointing or even a bit angry, because you were counting on them. That is why keeping promises matters so much.
asks: Why does a broken promise hurt?

faq.q: How can I remember my promises?
faq.a: Write a note, draw a picture, set a reminder with a grown-up, or put the thing by your bag the night before.
asks: Tell me about the Write it down

faq.q: When should I not make a promise?
faq.a: Do not promise things you cannot control, like: It will not rain on your party. And never promise to keep a secret that could hurt someone.
asks: Tell me about the Think first

faq.q: What if I really cannot keep a promise?
faq.a: Tell the person as early as you can, say sorry, and offer another way, like: I cannot come today, can I come on Saturday?
asks: What do I do if I break a promise?

faq.a: A pinky promise is when two people link their little fingers to seal a promise. In Japan it is called yubikiri, and children all over the world do it.

facts: In Japan, a pinky promise is called yubikiri, which means finger cutting.
Keeping small promises again and again is one of the main ways people build trust.
